clue.text: It's instrumental in broaching wine

indicators.note: to broach a cask is to pierce it, so the wine is opened up and something is put inside

blocks.note: claret is red Bordeaux wine
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone credits a tool with getting the cork out of a bottle of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broaching' sounds like opening the wine, and 'instrumental' like being helpful; claret is the British name for red Bordeaux.
explanation.definitionFit: A clarinet is a woodwind instrument, so the phrase about being instrumental is a playful description of it.

clue.text: Light (if you've nothing on) a squib

blocks.note: a lamp is a light
nothing is zero, the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tip about switching on a firework-like light when you are not wearing anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A squib is a short satirical piece, and a lampoon is a piece of writing that ridicules someone.

clue.text: Tail-enders put up to defend

blocks.note: to rear is to raise or put up
to guard is to defend

explanation.surface: The weakest batsmen are sent in to hold out and save the match.
explanation.walkthrough: Tail-enders are the last batsmen in a cricket team's order, but here the word just means those at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: The rearguard is the body of troops at the back of an army, the ones at the tail end.

clue.text: Character loved by Landor

blocks.note: first meaning: a person's basic temperament
second meaning: what the poet Walter Savage Landor said he loved first

explanation.surface: A literary note about a personality the poet Landor was fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: Landor's quatrain Dying Speech of an Old Philosopher begins 'Nature I loved, and next to Nature, Art'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's nature is their essential disposition, and Landor's famous line names it as the thing he loved most.

clue.text: Stuart repented and told her a different version

indicators.note: a different version of the words is the same material retold in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Stuart says sorry and gives his partner a new account of events.
explanation.walkthrough: James Francis Edward Stuart, son of James II, claimed the British throne and was called the Old Pretender.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Pretender was a member of the royal Stuart family, so a Stuart is a fair example-style definition.

clue.text: Vessels circulating for instance in pubs

indicators.note: something circulating goes round, so the abbreviation is turned back to front
in places the turned letters inside the drinking places

blocks.note: bars are pubs
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for instance

explanation.surface: Drinking glasses being passed around the pubs, say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessels' suggests glasses in the pub picture, but here they are boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Barges are flat-bottomed boats, and boats are vessels in the nautical sense.

clue.text: Slow footballer — give him room

blocks.note: a back is a defender in football
a ward is a room in a hospital

explanation.surface: A sluggish player on the pitch should be given more space.
explanation.definitionFit: Backward describes someone slow to develop or learn, a dated sense of lagging behind.

clue.text: Colour ran, spilt inside the store

indicators.note: something spilt is scattered, so those letters fall into a new order
inside puts the scattered letters within the colour

blocks.note: gray, the American spelling of grey, is a colour
the word ran rearranged

explanation.surface: Dye bled in the wash inside a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray is the American spelling of the colour; 'store' is not a shop but a storehouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A granary is a storehouse for grain, so it is a store in the sense of a depot.

clue.text: Veronica joins expedition to source

blocks.note: expedition can mean promptness or speed
a well is a source of water

explanation.surface: A woman called Veronica goes on a journey to find where a river begins.
explanation.walkthrough: Veronica looks like a woman's name but is the botanical genus of the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedwell is the common name for plants of the genus Veronica, small blue wild flowers.

clue.text: Disclose 19 pictures

blocks.note: 19 across is DEVIL, and an imp is a little devil
pictures collectively are art

explanation.surface: Reveal the devilish images.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart news is to make it known or tell it, the same as revealing it.

clue.text: Heard from river, a satisfied lark

indicators.note: heard means the words are taken by ear, so their spoken form matters, not their spelling

blocks.note: the Esk is a river in Scotland and northern England, a stays as written, and a satisfied debt has been paid

explanation.surface: Someone hears a satisfied songbird by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, ESK A PAID runs together into ESCAPADE. 'Lark' is not the bird but a prank.
explanation.definitionFit: A lark is a bit of mischief or fun, and an escapade is a daring or mischievous adventure.

clue.text: Bank beside American railway lines

blocks.note: the Dogger Bank is a sandbank in the North Sea
the El is an elevated railway in American cities such as Chicago

explanation.surface: A riverbank next to the tracks of a US railroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' looks like railway lines, but it means lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggerel is clumsy comic verse, and verse is written in lines.

clue.text: Super speller

blocks.note: first meaning: excellent, as old British slang
second meaning: one who casts spells

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as praise for someone good at spelling; speller is one who casts spells.
explanation.definitionFit: Wizard was British slang for marvellous, and a wizard is also a magician who works spells.

clue.text: By the sound of it, want to work

indicators.note: by the sound of it says to go by how a word is spoken, not by how it is spelt

blocks.note: to want is to need

explanation.surface: Someone seems keen to get a job.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means the answer is pronounced exactly like NEED.
explanation.definitionFit: To knead dough is to work it with the hands, pressing and folding it.

clue.text: Field Marshal Christopher North in good spirits

indicators.note: in places the compass letter inside the mood word

blocks.note: Kit is a short form of Christopher
cheer is a cheerful mood
N is the abbreviation for North

explanation.surface: Christopher North, the pen name of the writer John Wilson, is in a fine mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher North was a real pen name, which makes the pair look inseparable; here the two words are clued separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Kitchener was a British army Field Marshal, famous from the First World War recruiting poster.

clue.text: Fat round the middle, thin to port

blocks.note: spare can mean lean or thin
Tyre is an ancient port in Lebanon

explanation.surface: A paradox of fat and thin, with a nautical turn to the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the left side of a ship, but it is the harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: A spare tyre is the jokey British idiom for a roll of flab around the waist.

clue.text: He tattles, blowing up what's new

indicators.note: blowing up is exploding, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gossip who exaggerates the news.
explanation.definitionFit: The latest is the most recent news or fashion, exactly what someone means asking for news.

clue.text: What harshness, imprisoning fairy in a filthy hole

indicators.note: imprisoning shuts one thing inside another

blocks.note: the article a, taken as written
a sty is a filthy place, like a pigsty
a peri is a fairy in Persian mythology

explanation.surface: Outrage at a fairy being locked up in a dirty den.
explanation.walkthrough: A peri, a fairy from Persian legend, is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Asperity is roughness or severity of manner, so it is a direct synonym for harshness.

clue.text: Smartened scruffy shopkeepers

indicators.note: scruffy means untidy, so the letters are put into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Shop owners who were tidied up are still untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: Smartened and scruffy contradict each other, which hides the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tradesmen in British usage are shopkeepers or people who sell goods, especially those who deliver.

clue.text: Referee arrives, without incisiveness

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the abbreviation wraps round the other piece

blocks.note: arr. is the timetable abbreviation for arrives
bite is sharpness or incisiveness

explanation.surface: The referee turns up lacking any decisive edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking, but here it means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter is someone appointed to settle a dispute, like a judge or umpire.

clue.text: Was about to be a ghost

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word is read from the other end

blocks.note: lived means existed, was

explanation.surface: Someone was on the point of becoming a spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ghost' suggests a phantom, but it means a ghostwriter; to devil is to do hack work for another writer or a barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilling means doing unacknowledged work under someone else's name, which is what a ghostwriter does.

clue.text: Sincerely flatter the article penned by one friend

indicators.note: penned means shut in a pen, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a mate is a friend
it is the thing in question, the article

explanation.surface: A writer's friend has written something truly flattering.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the saying that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that copying someone is the most sincere compliment, so to copy is to flatter sincerely.

clue.text: Summits of Alpine peaks including, curiously enough, Snowdon

definitions.text: Summits of Alpine peaks including, curiously enough, Snowdon

indicators.note: the summit of each word is its top, which in a word means its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Mountain tops of the Alps, with the Welsh peak Snowdon oddly thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the apices it describes include Snowdon, the highest mountain in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Apices is the plural of apex, the top or peak of something, so summits of mountains are apices.

clue.text: Walk with unsteady gait to get hamper

blocks.note: first meaning: to limp along awkwardly
second meaning: to tie a horse's legs, so to impede

explanation.surface: Someone staggers off to fetch a picnic basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' suggests a basket, but it is the verb to hinder.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobble is both to limp and to restrict movement by tying the legs, hence to hinder.

clue.text: Forceful chap I met in Tours

indicators.note: being in tours means going round and round, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller recalls a pushy man they met in the French city of Tours.
explanation.walkthrough: Tours looks like the French city, but read as tours it means turns.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphatic means expressed with force and emphasis, so a synonym for forceful.

clue.text: It's well-known outside if I gave information

indicators.note: outside means one part goes round the other

blocks.note: something noted is famous
taken as written

explanation.surface: A common saying that someone passed on facts.
explanation.definitionFit: To notify is to inform someone formally, so having notified means having given information.

clue.text: Islander provides some secret anchorages

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: An island dweller knows of hidden harbours.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cretan is a native of Crete, a large Greek island, so someone from an island.

clue.text: Fish swallowing 18 get thinner

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside

blocks.note: a ray is a flat fish
18 down is ARBITER, a referee, shortened to ref

explanation.surface: A fish eats an official and somehow slims down.
explanation.definitionFit: To rarefy is to become less dense, as air does at altitude, so to grow thinner.

clue.text: Very large dog mums without prizes

indicators.note: the scan shows mums, but the newspaper printed turns, which means the dog is spun round to face the other way
without in its old sense means outside, so the turned word goes round the other

blocks.note: a setter is a breed of gun dog
OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: A huge dog at a show goes home without any awards.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan misreads the printed word turns as mums. 'Without' reads as lacking, but here it means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosettes are the ribbon badges awarded as prizes at shows, for example dog shows.
